summary: Defines the Basic HTTP authentication scheme, which transmits credentials as a user-id and password pair encoded with Base64. The encoding is not encryption, so it should only be used over a secure connection.

eli5.summary: You hand over your name and password in a note that only looks scrambled. It is fine if the note travels in a locked box.

questions: how does basic auth encode credentials
what is the charset parameter in basic auth
subtitle: How a browser sends a username and password in an HTTP header, and why that is only safe inside an encrypted connection.

tldr.problem: HTTP needs a simple way for a client to prove who it is to a server, and the original definition of the Basic scheme did not say which character encoding to use for the username and password.
tldr.mechanism: The client joins the user-id and password with a colon, encodes the result as octets, converts those to Base64 and sends it in an Authorization header. A new optional 'charset' parameter lets the server say it expects UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: The password still travels as cleartext, so the RFC says Basic is not secure without an external system such as TLS. It obsoletes RFC 2617 for this scheme.

today: RFC 7617 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2617 for the Basic scheme.

sections.title: What the Basic Scheme Is
sections.content:
RFC 7617 defines the Basic HTTP authentication scheme. The client sends credentials as a user-id and password pair, encoded using Base64. HTTP authentication schemes themselves are defined in RFC 7235.

The RFC is blunt about the limits: the scheme is not considered a secure method of user authentication unless it is used together with some external secure system such as TLS, because the user-id and password are passed over the network as cleartext.

The scheme was previously defined in RFC 2617. This document updates that definition and adds the charset authentication parameter to deal with internationalization. Together with three other documents, it obsoletes RFC 2617.
sections.eli5: Basic authentication is the simplest way to show a website who you are: you send your name and password along with your request. It is easy, but anyone who can peek at the message can read it.

sections.title: The Challenge and the Response
sections.content:
The model is that the client authenticates with a user-id and a password for each protection space, also called a realm. The realm value is a free-form string that can only be compared for equality with other realms on that server.

When a request lacks credentials, the server can reply with 401 (Unauthorized) and a WWW-Authenticate header field, for example WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="WallyWorld". A proxy can answer in the same way with 407 (Proxy Authentication Required) and Proxy-Authenticate.

In a challenge the scheme name is Basic, the realm parameter is REQUIRED and charset is OPTIONAL. No other parameters are defined: unknown ones MUST be ignored, and new ones can only be defined by revising the specification. Scheme and parameter names are matched case-insensitively.

Credentials use the token68 syntax from RFC 7235.
sections.eli5: The server says, "This area is called WallyWorld, show me your name and password." Your browser then answers with the secret note.

sections.title: Building the Credentials
sections.content:
To get authorization the client follows four steps. It obtains the user-id and password from the user, builds the user-pass by joining the user-id, a single colon and the password, encodes the user-pass into an octet sequence, and finally encodes those octets with Base64 into US-ASCII characters.

The RFC's example: user-id Aladdin and password open sesame give the header Authorization: Basic QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==.

Two rules follow from the colon. The user-id and password MUST NOT contain control characters. A user-id containing a colon is invalid, because the first colon separates user-id from password and text after it belongs to the password. The RFC notes that many user agents do not check for this, so recipients then treat part of the username as part of the password.
sections.eli5: You glue your name and password together with a colon, then run them through a scrambler that anyone can reverse. A name with a colon in it confuses the gluing.

sections.title: Character Encoding and the charset Parameter
sections.content:
The original definition never said how to turn the user-pass into octets. In practice, most implementations chose either a locale-specific encoding such as ISO-8859-1 or UTF-8. For backwards compatibility, RFC 7617 still leaves the default encoding undefined, as long as it is compatible with US-ASCII.

The new charset parameter appears only in challenges. It is purely advisory and tells the user agent which encoding the server expects. The only allowed value is "UTF-8", matched case-insensitively, meaning text is converted to Unicode Normalization Form C and encoded as UTF-8. Other values are reserved for future use.

Recipients MUST support all characters of the UsernameCasePreserved profile for the user-id (except the colon) and the OpaqueString profile for the password, both from RFC 7613.

Example: a challenge Basic realm="foo", charset="UTF-8", user test and a password of 123 followed by the pound sign U+00A3 produce Authorization: Basic dGVzdDoxMjPCow==.
sections.eli5: Different computers write letters like the pound sign in different secret codes. The server can now whisper, "please use the UTF-8 code," so both sides agree.

sections.title: Reusing Credentials
sections.content:
The authentication scope of an authenticated request is found by removing everything after the last slash in the path of its absolute URI. A client SHOULD assume that resources whose URIs share that prefix are in the same protection space.

A client MAY then send the Authorization header preemptively, without waiting for another challenge. The same applies to the Proxy-Authorization header toward a proxy.

With an authenticated request to http://example.com/docs/index.html, the URIs http://example.com/docs/ and http://example.com/docs/test.doc are in scope, while http://example.com/other/ and https://example.com/docs/ are not. A URI can belong to several scopes, and the RFC does not say which has priority.
sections.eli5: Once the guard has checked your ticket for one room in a hallway, you can show it again for the other rooms in that hallway without being asked.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The most serious flaw is that the user's password crosses the physical network in cleartext. Because of that, Basic SHOULD NOT be used, without enhancements such as HTTPS, to protect sensitive or valuable information.

Password reuse makes it worse. If a server lets users pick their own passwords, a leak can expose their accounts on other systems too. Basic is also open to spoofing by counterfeit servers, which can request a password, store it and feign an error. Servers ought to store passwords so that a leak does not make them trivially recoverable, avoiding plaintext or unsalted digests.

On internationalization, user-ids or passwords outside US-ASCII cause interoperability problems unless both sides agree on an encoding. The realm parameter is also a problem: RFC 7235 does not define a reliable way to carry non-US-ASCII characters in it.
sections.eli5: Sending a Basic password over an open connection is like shouting it across a crowded room. Use a private, locked channel, and keep the passwords you store hidden well.

sections.title: Deploying charset Safely
sections.content:
Appendix B explains why 'charset' is a hint and the default is not simply changed to UTF-8. Some sites default to a local encoding such as ISO-8859-1 and would break if user agents switched.

User agents that do not implement the parameter keep working and ignore it. Servers that need non-US-ASCII characters and can use UTF-8 opt in by adding charset to the challenge. Until all clients are upgraded, servers are likely to see both UTF-8 and legacy encodings and might fall back to the legacy encoding when UTF-8 processing fails.

Implicit retries need care: some subsystems treat repeated login failures as a possible credentials-guessing attack.
sections.eli5: Because some old websites still speak the old code, the server only asks for the new one. Computers that do not understand the request simply carry on as before.
